title: Albert von Kölliker at Würzburg: surviving histology collection and microscopy-teaching infrastructure
status: S-level collection survival + institutional teaching architecture; item-level slide-to-publication crosswalk open

primary_sources.institution: University of Würzburg, Institute for the History of Medicine
primary_sources.evidence: The medical-historical collections explicitly state that the histology collection from Anatomy survives and that its oldest sections are still by Albert von Koelliker.

primary_sources.institution: University of Würzburg, Institute of Anatomy and Cell Biology
primary_sources.evidence: Institutional history identifies Koelliker as professor from 1847-1903 and as a leading histologist/cell researcher; the present anatomical collection developed under this institute.

primary_sources.institution: University of Würzburg, Pathology Institute historical portal
primary_sources.evidence: The university history explicitly notes that Koelliker and Virchow transformed teaching by introducing practical microscopy courses.
The university states that Koelliker helped plan the 1883 Anatomical Institute and specifically requested large high windows so laboratories would receive as much light as possible for microscopy.

The university also preserves later Würzburg slide practice through Theodor Boveri preparations and a handwritten cardboard folder of twenty Ascaris slides, useful as a local institutional afterlife comparator rather than Koelliker attribution.

findings: The Würzburg medical-historical collection explicitly preserves a histology collection whose oldest sections are attributed by the institution to Albert von Koelliker.

Koelliker's microscopic research was tied to teaching practice: the university historical account identifies practical microscopy courses as an educational innovation associated with Koelliker and Virchow.
The physical institute itself encoded microscopy requirements: Koelliker's 1883 building planning included large high windows to maximise laboratory light for microscopic work.
This creates a surviving institutional chain from nineteenth-century histological preparations to practical microscopy pedagogy and a purpose-designed microscopy environment.

Later Würzburg survival of Boveri slide folders provides a local comparator for how prepared microscopic objects continued to be grouped, labelled and used in teaching/research within the same institutional ecology.

upgrade_decision.previous: A+ target: request inventory of slides attributed to Koelliker, labels and course/institute records
upgrade_decision.new: S-level collection survival and institutional microscopy-teaching architecture
upgrade_decision.reason: An official Würzburg collection description now explicitly confirms surviving histological sections by Koelliker, while independent university histories connect Koelliker to practical microscopy teaching and the physical design of microscopy laboratories.

guard: The current public pages do not provide item-level accession numbers, labels, dates, subjects or preparation techniques for the surviving Koelliker sections.
The broad Anatomical Collection also contains bones, wet preparations and later plastinated material; these should not be treated as Koelliker microscopic objects without inventory evidence.
The Boveri slides are a later Würzburg comparator and must not be folded into the Koelliker collection.
No direct surviving Koelliker slide-to-specific Handbuch/lecture/page crosswalk was closed in this pass.
next_exact_step: Request a bounded inventory/photo sample of the oldest Koelliker histology sections from the Institute for the History of Medicine, including current accession, verbatim label, tissue/species, date if present, mount format, storage order and any legacy catalogue number; then crosswalk two or three items to Koelliker's histology publications or microscopy-course documentation.
